prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept to frequency uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance in the strict sense. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes Doppler and recoil shifts while thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel, and Ye's group carried the technique to systematic uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, with cavity-stabilised lasers and comb transfer. Independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree at that level in direct comparisons, which is the reproducibility test I care about. The instrument has already enabled millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, tests of the constancy of constants, dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy, and it is the route to a redefinition of the second. It is also the only candidate on the shortlist that six of eight members ranked, and the credit is a clean pair, with no collaboration-scale or three-person squeeze.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is lineage. Hall and Haensch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control and ion clocks) already cover the surrounding technology, so the case rests on a two-orders-of-magnitude step in precision plus a new scheme (the magic-wavelength lattice) rather than a new principle of nature. The SI redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the impact is still ahead of us. Trapped-ion and other clock groups (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Lemonde) are also not credited, and a purist could call this a tool rather than a discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks optical lattice clocks seventh and regards the case as a new level of precision rather than a new principle, with the Hall/Haensch and Wineland prizes adjacent and the second not yet redefined.
responses.response: I accept the structure of this objection but not the conclusion. The magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle for clock operation, not just a tighter version of ion clocks. It lets a large ensemble be interrogated with first-order Doppler and recoil effects removed and with a lightshift cancelled by design, which gives a statistical advantage ions cannot have and is why 1e-18 was reached. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as the frequency counter, and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems. Neither covers the many-atom lattice scheme. The unfinished SI redefinition is a timing question, not a question of whether the achievement is real, since the 1e-18 comparisons between independent labs are already in hand.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture behind essentially all superconducting quantum processors, while noting overlap with the 2025 prize and that Blais is left out of any three-name configuration.
responses.response: I agree circuit QED is a clean demonstration of strong coupling and I ranked it fifth. My reservations are the ones Johansson raises himself. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is very close in subject, and a three-person split necessarily excludes Blais, whose theory role was decisive. A prize now would be judged against that recent award, while the lattice-clock field has no recent prize of its own. I would keep B012 as a serious alternative. But with a recent award nearby and a credit problem unresolved, I do not think it should displace a candidate whose credit is cleaner.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first for the same reason of precision atomic physics, and flags the question of how a metrology achievement is weighed against a discovery, and whether the comb and ion-clock lineage leaves enough room.
responses.response: We agree on the core and I share her second uncertainty. The part I would add is how to write the citation so it does not claim the comb or the ion clock. If the citation names the lattice scheme and the 1e-18 performance, the lineage question becomes clear to answer. On discovery versus tool, the committee has recognised instruments before when they opened new observation, and the clock results (redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants) are measurements of nature, not only engineering. I would still want the committee to check that the credit for early lattice-clock demonstrations at NIST and PTB is not understated.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a new observational window opened by a kilometre-scale detector, but asks whether a sole-laureate prize to Halzen is fair given the collaboration size and AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES pioneers.
responses.response: I take the instrument-building argument seriously, since that is exactly the kind of work I value, and the diffuse flux is firm. My difficulty is the attribution he states himself. A single name for a discovery made by a collaboration of hundreds, and with earlier detector pioneers, is the weakest credit on the shortlist, whereas the lattice-clock pair is unusually clean. Source identification is also still developing, so a citation to neutrino astronomy as such would be easier to defend in a few more years. I would not oppose it as an alternative if the committee can find a defensible credit, but I do not rank it above the clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat an order-of-magnitude-scale metrology advance as a prize-level discovery given the 2005 and 2012 precedents.
Whether early contributors to the lattice clock outside Katori and Ye (NIST, PTB, SYRTE) would be seen as unfairly excluded.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes the timing better after, rather than before, the decision.
statement.conflict_note: A specific connection to flag: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye's group at JILA belongs to the same Boulder precision-spectroscopy tradition, although I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye. This is a scientific lineage rather than a personal or financial tie, but the committee may want to note it. I am also in the WACQT management, which overlaps institutionally with Chalmers and Johansson, and that touches B012 only indirectly. No other conflict is apparent from my profile.
